name: Shaving cream

card.summary: A lather or cream that softens whiskers and lubricates the skin for a closer, smoother shave.
card.note: Fragrances and surfactants can irritate some skin.

quick.overview:
Shaving cream is applied before razor shaving to soften hair, hydrate it and lubricate the skin so the blade glides. It comes as aerosol foam, brushless cream or brush-lathered cream.

For looks, it supports a cleaner, smoother-shaven face or body with fewer nicks.
quick.how: It is applied to wet skin, often with hands or a brush, before shaving, then rinsed. Types include aerosol, brushless and lather creams; electric shaving uses alcohol-based dry-shave products instead.
quick.risks: Some products irritate or dry skin, and aerosol cans contain flammable propellants. Technique and razor matter as much as the cream.

lead: Shaving cream is a lather or cream applied before shaving to prepare the skin and hair. Most products are emulsions of oils, soaps or surfactants and water, sold in three main forms: aerosol foam, latherless (brushless) cream and lather cream used with a brush.[1]

It helps someone look better in a direct way: by lubricating the skin and hydrating whiskers, it lets the razor cut hair with less force, which supports a clean, even shave of the face, neckline, head or body, with fewer nicks and less irritation.[1][3] A smooth jawline or a crisp beard outline is one of the most common grooming steps in appearance-focused communities.

Shaving cream has a long history. A wood-alkali and animal-fat preparation was spread on beards in Sumer around 3000 BC, and the first modern brand, Barbasol, appeared in 1919.[1][4] No clinical trial has tested shaving cream as an appearance product; the surrounding literature concerns shaving-related skin conditions such as razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae).[5]

angle.text: Shaving cream gives the razor a slick, hydrated surface, supporting a clean shave of the face or body. People pair it with warm water and a sharp blade to get a smooth finish and a defined beard line.

paras: Three product types are common. Aerosol shaving cream (shaving foam) is a liquid lather cream dispensed from a pressurized can. Latherless or brushless creams produce no lather and are soap-free oil-in-water emulsions with humectants and wetting agents. Lather creams, usually used with a brush, are soap-based and foam when worked with water.[1] The term is also used for the lather made from a brush and a shaving soap.[1]

Typical lather creams contain roughly 20-30 percent soap (potassium or triethanolamine soaps), up to about 10 percent glycerine, and emollients, emulsifiers and foaming agents. Aerosols are diluted creams with hydrocarbon propellants of up to about 10 percent plus vegetable waxes and oils; the water in the formula offsets the propellants' flammability.[1] Products for electric or dry shaving work differently, containing 50-80 percent alcohol that dries the skin and stiffens whiskers so they stand up to the cutting head.[1]

The stated purpose of shaving cream is to soften hair by lubrication.[1] Hydrated hair needs much less force to cut, which is why wet-shaving guides recommend softening the beard with warm water or a hot towel first and then applying a lubricant such as cream, soap, gel or oil, often with a brush.[3] Hair hydration is also affected by pH, and manufacturers formulate with this in mind.[1]

A shaving brush adds to the effect. Wikipedia describes the brush as holding water that mixes with soap to make a moist, rich lather, which reduces razor skipping and dragging, and as lifting the whiskers so the razor needs less pressure.[6]

A mixture of wood alkali and animal fat was applied to beards in Sumer around 3000 BC.[1] Hard shaving-soap sticks were common into the early twentieth century, followed by tubes of oil and soft soap.[1] The modern shaving brush is traced to France in the 1750s; in the 1800s, folding straight razors made self-shaving practical and the brush became a status object.[6]

Frank Shields, a former MIT professor, developed the first modern shaving cream in Indianapolis in 1919, sold as Barbasol; he founded The Barbasol Company in 1920 and it owned the brand for 42 years.[1][4] Its 1920s and 1930s advertising used celebrity endorsers such as Babe Ruth, and radio spokesman Harry Frankel, known as Singin' Sam, was signed in 1931.[4] In the mid-1950s Robert P. Kaplan patented the first aerosol shaving-cream can for Barbasol, according to its Wikipedia page, while the general shaving-cream article credits Carter's Rise as the first pressurized can in 1949; within a decade aerosols held about two-thirds of the American market.[1][4] Pfizer bought the Barbasol company in 1962 and Perio, Inc. acquired the brand in 2001.[4]

Shaving gels were developed in the 1970s and Procter & Gamble patented a post-foaming gel in 1993.[1] CFC propellants were phased out in the 1990s over ozone damage and replaced with hydrocarbons such as pentane, propane, butane and isobutane.[1] The razors themselves changed in parallel: the double-edged safety razor was invented by King Camp Gillette in 1895 with commercial production from 1903, disposable razors took off after Bic introduced one in 1974, and multi-blade cartridges such as Gillette's Mach3 (1998) and Fusion (2006) followed.[3]

Wet shaving typically involves softening the skin with warm water, applying lather, shaving in several passes and finishing with an aftershave or an alum block or styptic pencil for small cuts.[3] Dry shaving with an electric razor needs no lather and causes fewer cuts, though it may not shave as closely.[3] Trimmers are used to shorten long beards before a blade shave.[3]

Many people who shave the head or body, or who keep a sharply edged beard, use shaving cream or soap for the same reason: a slick surface and softened hair give a cleaner finish. Hobbyist 'wetshaving' communities, which discuss soaps, brushes and creams, exist on forums such as Lemmy's c/wetshaving community; vintage cream advertisements, for example a 1936 Williams shaving cream ad in Life magazine, are also shared there.[7][8]

Brush-made lather is the traditional method. Soap or cream is worked into foam by agitating it with a wet brush, then applied to the face.[6] Bristle options include badger hair (graded pure, best, super and silvertip, with silvertip the rarest and most expensive and the most water-retentive), boar, synthetic nylon and horse hair.[6] In 2018 Procter & Gamble stopped using badger hair in its Art of Shaving products after a PETA investigation into badger-hair supply chains in China.[6] Synthetic brushes can produce rich lather with little soap and dry faster than natural hair.[6]

Wikipedia's shaving article describes razor burn as skin irritation appearing minutes after shaving and fading within hours to days; it is commonly associated with dull blades, dry shaving, excess pressure and shaving against the grain, and preventive measures include keeping skin moist, shaving with the grain, using light pressure and applying a soothing aftershave.[3] Shaving does not make hair grow back thicker or darker; cut hair only looks coarser because it lacks the natural tapered tip.[3]

Pseudofolliculitis barbae, or razor bumps, is persistent inflammation where regrowing hair curls back into the skin; it mainly affects people with curly or coarse facial hair.[3][5] Suggestions on its Wikipedia page include leaving about 0.5 to 1 mm of stubble, using single-blade or wire-wrapped razors with a fresh blade each time, shaving with the grain, softening the beard with a hot wet washcloth, and growing a beard as the most effective prevention.[5]

Product-specific risks are modest. Fragrances and surfactants can irritate some skin, and the hydrocarbon propellants in aerosol cans are flammable, although the water content of cream formulas reduces this.[1]
No studies found. A systematic review of pilonidal sinus surgery compared razor-and-cream hair removal with laser removal for recurrence, but that concerns a medical condition, not appearance.[2]

timeline.event: Wood alkali and animal fat preparation applied to beards in Sumer.[1]
The modern shaving brush emerges in France.[6]
King Camp Gillette invents the double-edged safety razor; commercial production begins in 1903.[3]
Frank Shields develops the first modern shaving cream, sold as Barbasol in Indianapolis.[1][4]
Carter launches Rise, the first pressurized can of shaving cream.[1]
CFC propellants are phased out in favour of hydrocarbons.[1]
Procter & Gamble patents a post-foaming gel.[1]
Perio, Inc. buys Barbasol from Pfizer.[4]
Procter & Gamble drops badger hair from its Art of Shaving brushes after a PETA investigation.[6]
